key_insight: The paper introduces Contextual Safety Filtering (CSF), a training-free way to make motion generation safer by interpreting safety rules in the context of the scene. Instead of judging an action in isolation, CSF checks whether the same motion could be safe or unsafe depending on what surrounds the agent.
problem_solved: Text-conditioned motion generators can produce the right motion mechanically, but they often ignore scene-dependent meaning and safety. Existing safeguards focus on the prompt, require labeled data, or rely on rigid geometric rules, so they miss cases where context changes whether an action is appropriate.
method: Grounds natural-language safety rules in scene context rather than prompt-only intent.
Applies a training-free filtering step to motion outputs from text-conditioned generators.
Uses context-aware reasoning to distinguish safe from unsafe motion even when the same action has different meanings in different scenes.
impact: CSF gives practitioners a practical safety layer that can be added without retraining motion models or collecting new labeled datasets. This is especially useful for human-robot interaction, character animation, and embodied AI systems operating in varied environments.
visual_elements: A split-scene comparison showing the same motion as safe in one context and unsafe in another.
A pipeline diagram: text prompt + scene context -> CSF filter -> accepted/rejected motion.
An icon-based safety checklist mapping natural-language rules to motion outputs.
A before/after illustration showing unsafe motion generation versus context-filtered motion.
paper_title: CSF: Contextual Safety Filtering for Motion Generators
paper_authors: Lizhi Yang, Yiling Hou, Yao Tang, Junheng Li, Daniel Weng
